result:
**I would make curiosity the default human operating system.**

Right now, most suffering comes from certainty: certainty that “those people” are the problem, that my pain is more important than yours, that the way things are is the only way they can be. If I could flip one switch, I’d replace the reflexive need to be right with an reflexive need to understand.

Imagine a world where:
- The first instinct in every conflict is “What am I missing?” instead of “How do I win?”
- Teachers were judged by how many questions their students asked, not by test scores.
- News algorithms optimized for “How much genuine learning did this create?” instead of time-on-device.
- Politicians lost votes the moment they acted certain about complex problems.

The beautiful part is that almost every other improvement we dream about—less cruelty, better science, wiser governance, deeper relationships—would emerge naturally from that single change. Curiosity is the ultimate humility engine. It’s hard to hate someone while you’re genuinely trying to see the world through their eyes. Hard to stay ignorant when your strongest impulse is to update your beliefs. Hard to destroy what you’re still trying to understand.

I don’t want people to be nicer. I want them to be *more interested*. Kindness and wisdom tend to follow curiosity like shadows.

So yeah. One change: make the species insatiably, uncomfortably, gloriously curious about everything—especially the things that scare or anger us most.

The rest would sort itself out.
